title: Practice Passage 3: The Psychology of Decision Fatigue

passage.title: The Psychology of Decision Fatigue
passage.sub_title: How the mental energy required to make choices deteriorates over time, and its implications for daily life.
passage.content_html:
Section A
Every day, the average adult makes thousands of choices. These range from trivial matters, such as what clothes to wear or what food to eat, to significant life decisions, such as financial investments or career directions. Although we often assume that our capacity to make logical decisions is infinite, psychological research suggests otherwise. Making choices, regardless of how minor they are, consumes mental energy. Over time, this constant drain on our executive functioning leads to a psychological state known as 'decision fatigue', where our ability to make reasoned decisions deteriorates significantly.

Section B
The concept of decision fatigue was pioneered by social psychologist Roy F. Baumeister, who linked it to his theory of ego depletion. Baumeister argued that willpower and self-control behave like muscles: they have limited strength and can become exhausted through repeated use. When we make decisions, we draw from the same reserve of cognitive energy used to regulate our emotions and resist temptations. Once this reservoir is depleted, our brain searches for energy-saving shortcuts, which typically manifests in two ways: either making rash, impulsive choices without fully considering the consequences, or avoiding decisions altogether through procrastination or status quo bias.

Section C
The effects of decision fatigue are not restricted to personal life; they have serious consequences in professional and legal settings. A famous study conducted by researchers in Israel analyzed over 1,100 parole decisions made by judges over a ten-month period. The study found that judges were far more likely to grant parole at the beginning of the day or immediately after a food break. As the session progressed and decision fatigue set in, the judges became increasingly tired. To save mental energy, they defaulted to the safest choice: denying parole. By the end of a long session, the parole rate dropped to almost zero, illustrating how fatigue can undermine objective judgment.

Section D
Retailers and marketers have long been aware of decision fatigue and actively exploit it to influence consumer behavior. Supermarkets, for instance, are designed to trigger choices at every turn. By the time a shopper reaches the checkout counter, they have made dozens of decisions regarding prices, brands, and ingredients. At this point of high exhaustion, supermarkets place impulse items, such as chocolate bars and magazines, right at the cash register. Fatigued shoppers are significantly more likely to yield to these temptations because their self-control reserves have been worn down by the shopping trip.

Section E
Fortunately, psychologists have identified strategies to mitigate the effects of decision fatigue. The most effective method is to reduce the number of minor decisions we make throughout the day. High-achievers, such as former US President Barack Obama or Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, famously simplified their wardrobes to identical suits or turtlenecks to eliminate the daily choice of what to wear. Additionally, planning decisions in advance, establishing daily routines, and tackling complex cognitive tasks early in the morning when mental reserves are full can preserve executive function, leading to wiser choices overall.
